What each unit, building and resource does — and how to use it
Pick a civilization for every seat on the New game screen. All civilizations field the same units and buildings — only these light bonuses differ.
The baseline realm. No bonuses and no penalties — the yardstick the other civilizations are measured against.
Sea raiders. Warships strike at strength 3, and transports and ports cost 5 less. Farms grow dearer faster and archers cost 4 more.
Desert merchants. Markets cost 4 less, mines pay 1 more, and the first farms come cheap. Warships cost 5 more and lumber camps pay 1 less per tree.
Defensive discipline. Towers and watchtowers cost 3 less, archers keep 1 coin of upkeep, and catapults march with range 3. Ports and transports cost 5 more.
Every turn you earn income and pay upkeep.

Each connected hex earns coins; each unit charges upkeep. If your treasury ever goes negative you go bankrupt and lose all your units — always keep income above upkeep. Tap the treasury at the top to see the full breakdown.
Take enemy or neutral land with your units.

A unit can capture an adjacent hex only when its Attack is greater than that hex\'s Defense — Defense 2 needs Attack 3. Towers, castles, capitals and nearby enemy units all raise defense. While a unit is selected, green chips mark hexes it can take and red chips show defenses that beat it — bring a stronger unit or a catapult to break through.
Combine soldiers into a stronger one.
Move two soldiers of the same tier together — or buy one onto another — to merge them into the next tier, up to Knight. Archers and catapults never merge.
Land must stay linked to your capital.
Only hexes connected to your capital earn income. If an enemy splits your territory, the cut-off part earns nothing and its units slowly starve — reconnect it quickly.
Your core fighters — four tiers from Peasant to Knight. Higher tiers hit harder but cost far more upkeep.

Buy one onto your own land. A fresh soldier can move anywhere inside your connected territory, or capture one adjacent hex whose defense is below its Attack. Merge two of the same tier for the next tier up.
Park it on ground you want to hold — it guards its own hex and every neighbour like a tower, but keeps pace with your army. It only attacks at Attack 1, so don\'t rely on it to capture.
Send it at towers and castles — it ignores building defense completely. It moves only 2 hexes per turn and can be intercepted, and it still loses to defending enemy units.

Buy it on the sea beside your port, then walk a unit onto it to embark. Sail up to 3 hexes per turn, park beside a beach and tap the shore to land — the passenger can even capture the beach with its own Attack. A boat alongside also feeds troops cut off from supply.

The navy\'s sword: move onto an enemy boat to sink it (ties go to you), or tap an adjacent enemy coastal hex to bombard it — the raid kills the garrison and razes any building except a capital. Towers shrug the bombardment off.

Buy it on the sea beside your port, sail it onto a fish shoal and leave it there — every turn it starts on the shoal, the catch is yours. It cannot fight and anything sinks it, so keep a warship near waters you share.
Built at sea beside your port
Grows your income. Place it next to your capital or an existing farm. Each farm costs a little more than the last, and one built on fertile ground earns extra.
Next to your capital or another farm
A cheap wall. Raises the defense of its own hex and all six neighbours, so an enemy needs a stronger unit to break in.
A stronger wall than the tower — defends its hex and all six neighbours. Use it to lock down a border or shield your capital.
Turns a gold vein into steady income. Scout for veins near your capital early and claim them.
Must be built on a gold vein
Earns more the more developed land surrounds it — one coin per producing neighbour, up to five. Place it in the middle of a cluster of your hexes, not on the frontier.
Build it beside a forest to earn from the trees around it (up to four). Bonus: trees next to a lumber camp stop spreading, so it also tames a growing forest.
A pure scout — no defense, but sees far through the fog. Only useful when Fog of War is switched on.

Build it on your coast. It opens the shipyard (boats are bought on adjacent sea), pays a little trade income, and — built overseas — feeds a whole colony that has no path to your capital. Lose the port and the colony starves.
On your own coast, next to the sea
Build it on your coast within two hexes of fish shoals — it earns from every shoal in range (up to three). The shoals are permanent; guard the coast and the coins keep coming.
On your coast, within two hexes of fish shoals

Buy it on a sea hex touching your land, then keep going — each span extends the chain. Troops walk it like a road (regions connect across it!), boats are blocked by it, and enemies can storm and keep it. Warship bombardment drops it back into the sea.
On sea, touching your land or bridge
The sea\'s gold vein. Capture the nearest coast and build a Fishery next to the shoal to harvest it.
It defends its own hex and neighbours. If an enemy captures it they loot half your treasury and it relocates to your largest region — losing your last territory loses the game.
Water divides the world — land units can never enter it. Ports, longboats and warships turn it into a highway.

Build a Port on your coast, buy a Longboat on the sea beside it, and walk a soldier aboard. Sail to a foreign shore and tap the beach to land — a strong passenger can storm defended ground. Keep the colony alive with a port of its own, and watch for enemy warships on the way.
A resource in the ground — worthless until you build a Mine on top of it, which turns it into steady gold.
Richer soil. Any hex here earns a little extra, and a farm built on it earns more still.
Blocks the hex\'s income. Move a unit onto it to clear it for a coin bonus, or build a Lumber camp nearby to profit from it. Left alone, forests slowly spread.
Marks where a unit died. It blocks income and grows into a tree after one round.
Land an enemy has severed from your capital. It earns no income and any units on it will starve — reconnect it fast.
A small hex-conquest game, built one turn at a time.

Fight & Conquer is a turn-based strategy game played on a hex map. You earn income from the land you hold, buy soldiers and merge them into stronger ones, wall your borders with towers, and take your neighbours\' territory — all while keeping your treasury out of the red.

It was inspired by Slay, by Sean O\'Connor, and by Antiyoy — two games whose quiet one-more-turn rhythm this one hopes to earn. Fight & Conquer is an independent project, written from scratch, and is not affiliated with or endorsed by either.

The rules live in a pure-Kotlin engine with no Android dependencies, so a turn plays out identically everywhere. The board is drawn in 3D with Google Filament, the interface is Jetpack Compose, and every piece was modelled low-poly in Blender and baked into the app.
A one-person hobby project, still young and still growing. Bug reports and ideas are very welcome.

Eight short lessons. One new idea each, and nothing on screen you have not been taught yet.
A quiet island, two farmhands, and six fields nobody has claimed. There is no money here and nothing to buy — only ground, and legs to walk it with.
Ground is the whole game. Everything after this is about getting more of it, and keeping it.
Tap one of your soldiers to pick it up.
The marked hexes are within reach. Tap one to take it.
Moving spends a soldier for the round. When both have gone, end your turn.
Take the rest of the marked fields.
Every hex you hold pays a coin a turn, and every soldier eats. Learn the arithmetic before someone makes you do it under pressure.
Income buys armies. Armies take ground. Ground pays income. That circle is the whole economy.
Tap the coin counter at the top to see where your money comes from.
Build a farm beside your capital — it pays far more than the bare hex under it.
Keep taking ground. Each hex is another coin a turn.
Watch the upkeep line. If it ever passes your income, your soldiers starve.
Two outposts, each with a defender. A single farmhand is not enough — but two of them, standing together, are something else entirely.
A merge costs nothing but the two soldiers you already had. It is the cheapest strength in the game.
Pick up a soldier: the shield numbers show how hard each hex is to take.
Two peasants in one territory merge into a spearman. Move one onto the other.
Attack must beat Defense outright — a tie is not enough. Take both outposts.
The pass between the two valleys changes hands with every raid. Stone holds ground that soldiers cannot — and the forest will pay for it.
A tower costs once and defends forever. A soldier costs every single turn.
Trees block income. Walk a soldier into one to clear it and pocket the timber.
Build a tower on the pass. It defends its own hex and all six neighbours.
Now keep all three pass hexes for four full rounds.
Your neighbour has overreached: a long arm of territory hanging off a single hex. Take the neck and the whole limb dies of its own weight.
You never had to fight the whole arm. You only had to fight one hex of it.
Territory cut off from its capital earns nothing, and its soldiers starve. Find the narrow hex.
Taking a capital pays you half of what is in its treasury. Finish them.
Two castles, three defence apiece, and a rival content to sit behind them. Knights can be bought. Walls have to be answered.
The catapult is slow, expensive and fragile. It is also the only thing on the board that does not care about walls.
Tap the castle. Three defence — no soldier you can afford beats that.
Build a catapult. It ignores buildings entirely, but only moves two hexes a turn.
An archer beside the catapult keeps it alive. Take both keeps.
There is no road to the far island. There is a harbour, a hull, and two hexes of open water.
Anything you can reach, you can take. The port is what decides what you can reach.
Build a port on the marked coast. Boats are sold at the water beside it.
Buy a transport, then walk a soldier onto it to load up.
Sail across and land on the far shore — a loaded boat can storm a beach directly.
The island is yours to take now. Finish it.
Two rivals, both richer than you. You cannot fight them at once — so do not. Buy time with a signature, and spend it well.
A pact is a tool, not a friendship. Everyone at that table knew it.
Open the diplomacy panel from the top bar. You cannot hold two fronts.
Offer a pact to the stronger neighbour and turn everything you have on the other.
Breaking a pact costs a quarter of your treasury. Sometimes that is a bargain.
Six chapters in one archipelago. Every one of them is a logistics problem before it is a fight.
The fleet is one hull and the army is one spearman, but the eastern beach is empty and the tide is right. Get ashore, and stay ashore.
Landing was never the hard part. Being there the following morning was.
Walk a soldier onto the transport to load it, then sail.
Land on the marked sand. A loaded boat can take a beach outright.
Soldiers beside one of your own boats never starve. Keep the hull close and hold the beach.
A relief squadron reaches the anchorage.
Fog on the water, and one watchtower that can see through it. Lose the beacon and the channel belongs to whoever wants it.
You held a hex worth nothing at all, and it was the only thing on the map that mattered.
You can only see what your ground, your soldiers and your towers can see.
The beacon watches six hexes in every direction. It must not fall.
Twelve rounds. Keep the beacon and keep breathing.
A raider slips out of the fog.
Raiders have been crossing the channel for a season. The council wants three hulls on the bottom of it.
At sea, the tie goes to whoever moved first. Remember that when you are the one being hunted.
Build a warship. It is the only thing that can sink another boat.
Sail onto a raider to sink it — at sea, an equal fight goes to the attacker.
A raider is sighted in the channel.
A second raider runs the channel.
The last of the pack breaks cover.
Two hexes of water, and a treasury that will not stretch to a fleet. Masons are cheaper than admirals.
A bridge is ground. It is walked on, fought over, and it does not sink.
Build a bridge onto the water beside your coast, then extend it hex by hex.
The bridge is road now. March across and finish them.
The admiral holds the eastern isle. The southern flag holds everything else, and is watching to see which way this goes.
One rival down. The other watched the whole thing and learned from it.
Two rivals, one of you. The diplomacy panel is in the top bar.
The admiral is the target. The southern flag is not — yet.
Every island, every channel, both rivals. No clock, no favours, nothing held back.
The archipelago is yours, salt and stone and all of it.
Everything the campaign taught you is on this board. So is everything it taught them.
These shoals pay twice — a Fishery on the coast works them from two hexes out, and a fishing dory anchored on the shoal hauls its own catch.
A succession war fought entirely on land. What ground earns, what it costs to hold, and what happens when you run out.
Before the war, the harvest. Rich soil doubles what a farm returns, and the crown will be paid for long before it is fought for.
Wars are won in the accounts a year before they are won in the field.
The marked hexes are rich soil. A farm there earns far more than one anywhere else.
A market pays for every producing hex around it. Put one inside your territory, not on its edge.
Keep building. Thirty-two coins a turn is the target.
Both claimants have declared against you at once. There is nothing to win here. There is only the levy, four rounds out, and everything between now and then.
You did not beat them. You outlasted them, which counts the same in the chronicles.
Two enemies, one of you. Trade ground for time and keep your capital covered.
The levy musters at the marked hex. Hold until it arrives.
Fourteen rounds. Nothing else is asked of you.
Three seams of gold in the middle of the map, and neither claimant has the sense to be first to them. Take that back.
Ore in the ground is worth nothing. Ore under a mine pays for armies.
The marked hexes are gold seams. Take all three.
A mine only stands on a seam — and it earns six a turn while it does.
Three seams, three mines. Then the treasury does the rest.
Everything has narrowed to the bastion above the throne room. Ground elsewhere is a luxury. That hex is not.
The wall held. Very little else did, and it did not matter.
The bastion is the mission. Lose it and nothing else counts.
You cannot hold two fronts. Buy one of them off.
Sworn swords ride in through the postern.
A line of castles across the waist of the continent, built by someone who never expected siege engines.
Walls are an answer to soldiers. They were never an answer to engineering.
Two keeps, three defence each. Soldiers will not do it.
Build a catapult. Walls mean nothing to it — enemy soldiers still do.
Take both keeps and the line is broken.
Three claims, one crown, and no more room for arrangements. Settle it.
The succession is settled. The crown was always iron; now it is yours.
No clock, no levy, no favours. Only the board.
